description:
What does Revelation’s promise that God’s servants will see his face actually mean? Returning to the question left open in the previous meeting, Wesam Saad identifies this future vision with Jesus Christ revealed in glory. He begins with the problem of sin: biblical encounters with divine glory expose human unholiness. The resurrection, he explains, removes the remaining corruption that prevents believers from standing before Christ without fear of destruction.

Saad connects Jesus’ declaration that seeing him is seeing the Father with Hebrews’ description of the Son as the radiance of God’s glory. He maintains the distinction between Creator and creature, arguing that created beings do not become able to see God’s invisible essence directly. Questions about angels and earlier appearances of God help him distinguish seeing God through the Son from seeing the fullness of Christ’s glory without its being veiled.

The emphasis turns from explanation to longing. God’s presence, rather than heavenly surroundings alone, is presented as the source of lasting satisfaction. Saad encourages listeners to anticipate personal fellowship with Christ. He introduces the further question of how Christ will satisfy his people in the eternal state, leaving its fuller answer for the following session.

questions.question: Whose face does Saad understand believers to see in the promised future?
questions.answer: He understands the promise as beholding Jesus Christ, the second person of the Trinity, with his glory revealed. He connects seeing the Son with seeing the Father, rather than imagining separate bodily faces for the Father and the Spirit.

questions.question: Why does the study connect seeing God with the removal of sin?
questions.answer: Saad points to the fear and collapse described in encounters with divine glory, including John’s response to the risen Christ. He argues that redemption and resurrection bring the holiness needed for this future vision. He describes the absence of selfishness, pride and other remaining sinful impulses as part of that hope.

questions.question: How do John 14:9 and Hebrews 1:3 support his explanation?
questions.answer: Jesus’ statement that whoever has seen him has seen the Father supplies the central connection. Hebrews describes the Son as the radiance of God’s glory and the exact representation of his nature. Saad uses these passages to explain why seeing God is focused on Christ.

questions.question: Does this future vision erase the distinction between God and created beings?
questions.answer: Saad insists that the Creator–creature distinction remains. In his explanation, neither humans nor angels become God or step outside their created existence to see God’s invisible essence directly. God makes himself known to creatures through the Son; that relationship does not turn them into the Creator.

questions.question: How does he respond to the passage about angels seeing the Father’s face?
questions.answer: He reads Matthew 18:10 alongside Jesus’ words about seeing the Father through him. He therefore distinguishes God’s invisible essence from the revelation of God in Christ, which sinless angels can behold. When asked why angels cover their faces, he offers possible explanations such as reverence without claiming to settle the reason.

questions.question: Why do earlier appearances of God not overturn his argument?
questions.answer: Saad distinguishes God genuinely appearing to people from revealing the full extent of his glory. He says that historical manifestations, including Christ’s earthly appearances, do not establish that sinful people could bear that unrestricted glory. His account of the future places the removal of sin alongside an unveiled encounter with Christ.

questions.question: What makes God’s presence central to the hope of heaven?
questions.answer: The study presents God himself as the greatest gift and the source from which other heavenly pleasures receive their significance. Saad uses the language of thirst and satisfaction to encourage longing for personal fellowship with Christ, including being able to speak with him and receive his response.

questions.question: What question is introduced but not fully answered at the close?
questions.answer: Saad asks how Christ will satisfy believers in the eternal state. Participants offer thoughts about restored relationship, freedom from sin and fullness of joy. He welcomes those contributions but postpones his fuller explanation until the next session, so they should not be treated as a completed teaching outline.
